title: The Farmer and His Sons
text:
A farmer who knew he was dying worried about his sons. They were idle young men, and he feared that once he was gone they would let the farm go to ruin.

He called them to his bedside. "My sons," he said, "I am about to leave this world. Everything I have to give you is in the vineyard. Search there and you will find it." Then he died without saying more.

Convinced their father had buried a treasure, the sons went out with spades and mattocks. They dug up every corner of the vineyard. They turned the soil row by row, deep and thoroughly, again and again. They found no pot of gold, no hidden chest, nothing at all.

But the vines, with their roots so well loosened and the earth so well worked, produced a harvest richer than any the farm had seen in years. When the sons sold the grapes, they finally understood what their father had left them. The treasure was the work itself.

La Fontaine retold the fable in 1668, with an old ploughman telling his children that a treasure lies hidden in the field.
lesson: The most valuable inheritance is not money but the habit of steady work. Give children reasons to put their hands to something that grows.
source: Aesop's Fables (Perry 42); Jean de La Fontaine, Fables, Book V, 9 (Le Laboureur et ses Enfants)
